A free trade area covering most of Africa, founded by an agreement signed in Kigali, Rwanda, on 21 March 2018. The African Union brokered it, and 44 of its 55 members signed that day. It came into force in May 2019, once 22 countries had ratified it, and trading under it began on 1 January 2021. Its secretariat sits in Accra, Ghana.

By number of members it is the largest free trade area after the World Trade Organization, spanning about 1.3 billion people. Members agree to drop tariffs on most goods over 5 to 13 years, depending on how developed they are. The longer aims are a single market, freer movement of money and workers, and a customs union.

The idea goes back to Pan-Africanism and leaders like Kwame Nkrumah, who argued that small, divided states would stay weak. African countries still trade far more with Europe and Asia than with each other, partly because colonial railways ran from mines and farms to the ports. Slow borders and poor roads hold the plan back.
